definition: Fathom means to understand something deeply — to get to the bottom of it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word fathom. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know fathom should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Naval historians still cannot fathom why the flagship turned into the storm when every signal ordered her home.
To follow an argument is just to keep up with it step by step — far short of fathoming it.
To grasp an idea stops short of fathoming it: you hold the main point, but the bottom is still out of reach.

Comprehend is the formal word for full understanding — a reader comprehends a passage and can restate its point. Fathom digs further down and usually appears in the negative: to fathom something is to reach its very bottom, which is exactly what keeps failing when the word shows up.

Decipher means to decode something hidden — bad handwriting, a cipher, a garbled signal — and once decoded it turns plain. Fathom needs nothing decoded: the thing sits in plain sight, and what resists you is its depth. You decipher a coded note; you fathom why it was written.
to take the wrong meaning from what's in front of you
to mix ideas up instead of making sense of them

Fathom is Old English faethm, the span of two outstretched arms — about six feet. Sailors measured depth by paying out rope one arm-span at a time, so 'to fathom' became to reach the very bottom of a thing. No other English word descends from it.
Fathom means to understand something deeply — to get to the bottom of it.
Rosa could not fathom the appeal of the mobile game her roommates played for hours — she tapped the same three buttons they did and felt nothing but the minutes leaving.
Fathom digs deeper than 'understand': an old sailor's word for sounding the sea's depth, it means getting all the way to the bottom of something — which is why it usually appears when someone can't.
neutral, usually in the negative
Fathom almost always travels with can't, couldn't, or hard to — it flags depths that resist understanding.
For ordinary comprehension, 'grasp' or 'follow' will do; fathom promises the very bottom of the thing.

In 1348, the village of Wharram Percy had a church, a mill, and sixty households; within a generation it stood empty.
Archaeologists can list everything about the leaving except the reason for it.
The dig has recovered account books, unbroken pottery, even a plow left mid-field -- a record so complete that researchers can restate the villagers' final season week by week.
What no one can fathom is why families who had just brought in a good harvest walked away from all of it.
The bottom of the question, one historian wrote, lies deeper than any trench the team can dig.
